newsitem.title: UK: BA, unions seek peace talks to end strike.
newsitem.headline: BA, unions seek peace talks to end strike.

text.p: In the midst of a three-day strike by flight attendants, British Airways and unions representing its disgruntled staff offered Friday to meet for talks over the weekend to head off further strikes.
Hundreds of flights and thousands of passengers have been stranded by the strike, which started Wednesday and was expected to end early Saturday.
BA Chief Executive Bob Ayling wrote Friday to Bill Morris, the leader of the main transport union, urging him to meet for new talks.

Ayling also asked to see the union's proposals to achieve the 42 million pounds ($70.9 million) in savings the airline is seeking in its cabin crew operation, BA's director of operations Mike Street said.

"BA goes into these talks in the spirit of getting a solution and in the talks offered by (the union) we now have a firm commitment ... to the savings that we require from the restructuring," Street told ITN television.
The union has pledged to help the airline find the 42 million pound savings, but it is not prepared to have new terms and conditions imposed on employees.

BA faces a potentially explosive two-pronged assault from cabin crew and catering staff, who Thursday night rejected company proposals in a separate dispute over the sale of its Heathrow airport catering unit.

The catering union meets Monday to decide whether to call its own 24-hour strike, which may include check-in staff and baggage handlers. If cabin crew and ground staff combined to strike, BA would face huge disruptions.

The union's Morris said he wanted talks to solve both disputes. "What we want to do is find a solution to the two problems," Morris, general secretary of the Transport and General Workers Union, told BBC radio.
"That is why we are inviting the airline to come along with us to explore all the options to find a sensible and long lasting resolution to the problems we face," he added.
BA said it was getting more flights away on the last full day of the strike and expected to have about 80 percent of its normal network services operating Friday.
Cabin crew have threatened to call another 72-hour strike this month unless an agreement is reached.
According to BA, of about 7,000 BA cabin crew union members, approximately 250 were officially on strike on Friday while another 1,600 cabin crew were off sick.

Union leaders and left-wing Labour members of Parliament accused BA of intimidating staff by threatening them with loss of travel perks, promotion prospects and of taking legal action. BA rejects the charge.
BA will not say how much the strike has cost the airline, one of the world's biggest, but the union estimated the bill already exceeded 100 million pounds ($160 million).
